# Family Psycho-Cyber Risk Model (FPCRM)

## Overview
**Family Psycho-Cyber Risk Model (FPCRM)** is a human-centric cybersecurity risk model designed to quantify and govern **family-level digital risk** by integrating **family psychological dynamics** with **cybersecurity behavioral indicators**.

FPCRM explicitly avoids network/infrastructure framing and focuses only on the **family psyche → cyber exposure** pathway.

## Core Assumption
In family environments, a large portion of cybersecurity risk is *psychologically generated* (trust misplacement, dependency, boundary weakness, emotional pressure), and only later becomes *technically observable* (account exposure, unsafe clicks, permission abuse, password sharing).

## Scope (Included)
- Family psychology dynamics: trust, dependency, boundaries, emotional pressure, impulsivity
- Behavioral cybersecurity: passwords, account exposure, link-click susceptibility, app permissions, device/account sharing
- Governance recommendations: protection, education, restriction, containment (non-network)

## Explicitly Excluded
- Network infrastructure (routers, protocols, IDS/IPS)
- Enterprise security models
- Clinical diagnosis / medical labeling
- Real sensitive family data (the model supports synthetic / simulated data)

## Outputs
- **Unified Risk Score (0–100)**
- **Risk Class**: Low / Moderate / High / Critical
- **Family Governance Action**: Advisory / Monitor & Educate / Restrict & Correct / Contain & Support

## Intended Use
Research, education, conceptual simulation, and the development of family-centered cybersecurity frameworks.

instances.usage:
### Example Use (Conceptual)

1) Assign values (0–1) for the psychological and behavioral indicators (synthetic or survey-based).

2) Compute PsyScore and CyberScore.

3) Generate a Risk Score and map it to a governance action (education / restriction / containment).

> FPCRM is designed to be implemented as a lightweight scoring engine inside a notebook or a future app interface.

# Qwen3-Coder-Next

## Highlights

Today, we're announcing **Qwen3-Coder-Next**, an open-weight language model designed specifically for coding agents and local development. It features the following key enhancements:  

- **Super Efficient with Significant Performance**: With only 3B activated parameters (80B total parameters), it achieves performance comparable to models with 10–20x more active parameters, making it highly cost-effective for agent deployment.
- **Advanced Agentic Capabilities**: Through an elaborate training recipe, it excels at long-horizon reasoning, complex tool usage, and recovery from execution failures, ensuring robust performance in dynamic coding tasks.
- **Versatile Integration with Real-World IDE**: Its 256k context length, combined with adaptability to various scaffold templates, enables seamless integration with different CLI/IDE platforms (e.g., Claude Code, Qwen Code, Qoder, Kilo, Trae, Cline, etc.), supporting diverse development environments.

![image/jpeg](https://qianwen-res.oss-accelerate-overseas.aliyuncs.com/Qwen3-Coder-Next/benchmarks.png)

![image/jpeg](https://qianwen-res.oss-accelerate-overseas.aliyuncs.com/Qwen3-Coder-Next/swebench_pro.png)


## Model Overview

**Qwen3-Coder-Next-** has the following features:
- Type: Causal Language Models
- Training Stage: Pretraining & Post-training
- Number of Parameters: 80B in total and 3B activated
- Number of Parameters (Non-Embedding): 79B
- Hidden Dimension: 2048
- Number of Layers: 48
  - Hybrid Layout: 12 \* (3 \* (Gated DeltaNet -> MoE) -> 1 \* (Gated Attention -> MoE))
- Gated Attention:
  - Number of Attention Heads: 16 for Q and 2 for KV
  - Head Dimension: 256
  - Rotary Position Embedding Dimension: 64
- Gated DeltaNet:
  - Number of Linear Attention Heads: 32 for V and 16 for QK
  - Head Dimension: 128
- Mixture of Experts:
  - Number of Experts: 512
  - Number of Activated Experts: 10
  - Number of Shared Experts: 1
  - Expert Intermediate Dimension: 512
- Context Length: 262,144 natively

**NOTE: This model supports only non-thinking mode and does not generate ``<think></think>`` blocks in its output. Meanwhile, specifying `enable_thinking=False` is no longer required.**

For more details, including benchmark evaluation, hardware requirements, and inference performance, please refer to our [blog](https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3-coder-next), [GitHub](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-Coder), and [Documentation](https://qwen.readthedocs.io/en/latest/).



## Citation

If you find our work helpful, feel free to give us a cite.

```
@techreport{qwen_qwen3_coder_next_tech_report,
  title        = {Qwen3-Coder-Next Technical Report},
  author       = {{Qwen Team}},
  url          = {https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-Coder/blob/main/qwen3_coder_next_tech_report.pdf},
  note         = {Accessed: 2026-02-03}
}
```

instances.usage:
## Quickstart

We advise you to use the latest version of `transformers`.

The following contains a code snippet illustrating how to use the model generate content based on given inputs. 
```python
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import kagglehub

model_name = kagglehub.model_download("qwen-lm/qwen3-coder-next/transformers/qwen3-coder-next")

# load the tokenizer and the model
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
  model_name,
  torch_dtype="auto",
  device_map="auto"
)

# prepare the model input
prompt = "Write a quick sort algorithm."
messages = [
  {"role": "user", "content": prompt}
]
text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
  messages,
  tokenize=False,
  add_generation_prompt=True,
)
model_inputs = tokenizer([text], return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)

# conduct text completion
generated_ids = model.generate(
    **model_inputs,
    max_new_tokens=65536
)
output_ids = generated_ids[0][len(model_inputs.input_ids[0]):].tolist() 

content = tokenizer.decode(output_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)

print("content:", content)
```

**Note: If you encounter out-of-memory (OOM) issues, consider reducing the context length to a shorter value, such as `32,768`.**

For local use, applications such as Ollama, LMStudio, MLX-LM, llama.cpp, and KTransformers have also supported Qwen3.

## Deployment

For deployment, you can use the latest `sglang` or `vllm` to create an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint.

## Best Practices

To achieve optimal performance, we recommend the following sampling parameters: `temperature=1.0`, `top_p=0.95`, `top_k=40`.

> [!Note]
> This repository contains the **FP8-quantized Qwen3-Coder-Next** model checkpoint for convenience and performance. 
> The quantization method is "fine-grained fp8" quantization with block size of 128. 
> You can find more details in the `quantization_config` field in `config.json`.
>
> In addition, the experimental results presented in this model card are obtained from the original bfloat16 model prior to FP8 quantization.
